title: How I Hear Music
subtitle: A Personal Music Taste Archive
tagline: A record of songs, sounds, artists and the moments that stay.
quote: Every element needs a reason to exist.
heroNote: A listening method, not a ranking.

evidenceLabels.IN_THE_LIST: Present in the listener's list; not automatically a favorite.

listeningOrder.name: Melody
listeningOrder.note: The first barrier: the hardest gate, though not an absolute veto.

listeningOrder.name: Production / Arrangement
listeningOrder.note: Movement, shape, timing and the information that returns on replay.

listeningOrder.name: Timbre + Lyrics

listeningOrder.name: Vocal ability
listeningOrder.note: Appreciated, but never the point by itself.

qualifications: It depends on what catches attention.
Resonance is real, but it is not a number.
firstGateCopy: Melody opens the door. Arrangement makes me stay. Details make me return.
methodCopy: A song can be minimal or maximal, innovative or inherited, unified or full of detours. The format is never the rule. The question is whether every choice feels intentional and alive.

signals.title: A melody with remaining life
signals.text: Not necessarily difficult—just not exhausted by the first listen.

signals.title: Purposeful movement
signals.text: A second chorus can become something else. A late section can reveal why the earlier one existed.

signals.title: A human take
signals.text: Technique should expand expression, not erase the person inside the voice.

surpriseFactor.title: The surprise factor
surpriseFactor.statement: I don't need a song to be complicated. I need it to keep becoming something.

stages.label: Setup
stages.detail: A world, a melody, a promise.

stages.label: Develop
stages.detail: The song reveals more of its internal logic.

stages.label: Surprise
stages.detail: A chord, harmony, drum turn or vocal event arrives at the right moment.

stages.label: Payoff
stages.detail: An earlier idea returns with a different weight.

surpriseFactor.latePayoffNote: A great ending raises the whole evaluation a bit; it does not rescue a weak foundation.

humanVoice.title: The human voice
humanVoice.refusal: Obvious Auto-Tune or pitch correction replacing human presence: totally unacceptable.
humanVoice.timbreNote: No fixed timbre preference. The question is whether the voice belongs to the song.

origin.lede: “How songs can be showed like that.”
origin.text: The first active exploration began after seeing 单依纯 present Forever Young on stage. The discovery was not only a voice, but that a song and its presentation are not the same thing: arrangement, phrasing, timbre, space and interpretation can make the same work feel like another world.
origin.producerNote: The producer matters here too: singer and producer are co-authors of a presentation.

interview.title: An interview with a listener
interview.intro: The archive is not a verdict. It is a conversation with the parts of a song that keep asking to be heard.
interview.aside: Answers assembled from the listening conversations behind this archive.

questions.question: What has to happen before a song becomes yours?
questions.answer: Melody is the first gate. It is the hardest one to pass, but not an absolute veto. A melody can reveal itself slowly, as long as there is enough life left for me to discover.

questions.question: Do you need a song to be complicated?
questions.answer: No. I can accept something almost bare or something densely produced. Complexity is not a virtue by itself. The real question is whether every chord, texture and change has a reason to exist.

questions.question: What makes you return after the first listen?
questions.answer: Movement. I like a song that keeps opening small doors on replay: a harmony I missed, a groove that shifts, a vocal layer, a motif that comes back with a different weight. I do not need constant novelty; I need meaningful information.

questions.question: What kind of surprise feels earned?
questions.answer: A surprise should belong to the song. A late payoff can raise the whole evaluation, especially when an earlier idea returns or an arrangement suddenly explains itself. But a beautiful ending cannot rescue a weak foundation.

questions.question: Where does vocal ability fit in your priorities?
questions.answer: I appreciate technique, but I do not treat technique as the point. I want a voice to feel present, placed and alive inside the song. An imperfect take can be more convincing than a polished take that has lost the person.

questions.question: What is non-negotiable about a vocal recording?
questions.answer: Harmony and vocal arrangement are welcome in almost any form. What I cannot accept is obvious Auto-Tune or pitch correction replacing human presence. The tools should expand expression, not erase the singer.
questions.note: BOUNDARY / NO SUBSTITUTE FOR A PERSON

questions.question: Do you like melodies that take time to find?
questions.answer: Yes, sometimes. The B-type song can become rewarding because its melody arrives through repeated listening. But I am not trying to make music difficult on purpose. I want a song to have a life beyond its first impression.

questions.question: How does one song lead you to an album?
questions.answer: Often by accident: I hear one song, then look for the record, then begin at Track 1. I want to meet the album in its own order, even when the song that brought me there is somewhere else.

questions.question: What makes an album great?
questions.answer: One extraordinary song can make the whole album matter to me. Ten songs that hold a steady 8 can do it too. An album may be unified or varied, innovative or deliberately continuous; the standard is not uniformity, but intention.

questions.question: Do you listen only for structure?
questions.answer: No. I can follow the details of an arrangement and still see a picture, a story or a version of myself. The analytical and imaginative ways of listening are not opposites; they can happen at the same time.

questions.question: What happens when a song really becomes yours?
questions.answer: I loop it. I do not ration a song to avoid getting tired of it. If I love a particular section, I can point to that moment, but I do not always need to explain the whole taste judgment to someone else.

questions.question: Can you separate an artist from the work?
questions.answer: Yes. An artist can change, and my view of that person can change, without rewriting what an earlier work did for me. The past song remains a past experience with its own shape and meaning.

discovery.title: My music discovery
discovery.intro: One song gets me in. Then I find the album. Then I start from Track 1.
discovery.albumPrinciple: One astonishing song can make an album great. So can ten songs that hold a steady 8.
albumQualifiers: Outliers are welcome when they have a reason

notRequirements.title: Not a requirement
notRequirements.intro: Perfect vocals, complex chords, constant innovation and album uniformity are not requirements. But every choice needs a reason.

rituals: I loop songs that become mine. I do not deliberately ration them to avoid getting tired.
I notice details when the music makes me listen closer—not in order to perform analysis.
Music can create a picture, story or self-projection; it can also be heard through its structure.
I can point to the moment I love without needing to win the argument about it.
principles: Technical quality and personal love are different records.
A later change in an artist does not retroactively change a work already made.

closing.note: Not because it is perfect. Because something in it keeps changing every time I listen.
